questions.text: What is a crate in Rust?

answers.text: The smallest amount of code the Rust compiler considers at one time
Any directory containing Cargo.toml
Only a library published on crates.io
A group of modules that must contain several files

questions.explanation: A crate is the smallest amount of code the compiler considers at one time; even a single file passed to rustc is treated as a crate.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Packages and Crates, pp. 158–159

questions.text: Which statements about crate types are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: A binary crate compiles to an executable
A binary crate must have a main function
A library crate is intended to provide functionality for other projects
A library crate must contain main

questions.explanation: Binary crates produce runnable programs and have main. Library crates provide functionality to other projects and do not require main.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Packages and Crates, pp. 158–159

questions.text: What is a package in Cargo?

answers.text: One or more crates that provide functionality and are described by Cargo.toml
Only one binary crate with no libraries
Any module declared with pub mod
A source file passed to rustc

questions.explanation: A package groups one or more crates and contains a Cargo.toml describing how they are built.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Packages and Crates, pp. 158–159

questions.text: Which restrictions apply to the contents of a Cargo package? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: A package must contain at least one crate
A package may contain any number of binary crates
A package may contain at most one library crate
A package must contain both a binary and a library crate

questions.explanation: The material permits any number of binary crates, at most one library crate, and requires at least one crate of either kind.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Packages and Crates, pp. 158–159

questions.text: How does Cargo treat `src/main.rs` in an ordinary package?

answers.text: As the crate-root module of a binary crate with the same name as the package
As the package configuration file
As the crate-root module of a library crate
As a file Cargo ignores unless Cargo.toml explicitly names it

questions.explanation: By convention, Cargo treats src/main.rs as the root of a binary crate whose name matches the package name.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Packages and Crates, pp. 158–159

questions.text: Which Cargo conventions about crate files are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: src/lib.rs is the crate-root module of a library crate
If src/main.rs and src/lib.rs both exist, the package contains a binary and a library crate
Files in src/bin can form separate binary crates
Having src/lib.rs forbids src/main.rs

questions.explanation: Cargo recognizes src/lib.rs as the library root, src/main.rs as a binary root, and each file in src/bin can be a separate binary crate.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Packages and Crates, pp. 158–159

questions.text: What is a crate-root module?

answers.text: The source file from which the compiler starts building the crate's root module
The first public module alphabetically
Any file named mod.rs
Only Cargo.toml

questions.explanation: The crate root is the source file from which Rust starts forming that crate's module tree.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Packages and Crates, pp. 158–159

questions.text: Which tasks does Rust’s module system solve? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Organizing code
Controlling scope
Hiding or exposing paths to items
Automatically managing reference lifetimes

questions.explanation: Chapter 7 connects modules and use with organization, scopes, and path visibility; lifetimes are covered elsewhere.

questions.text: After declaring `mod garden;` in the crate root, where can the compiler find the `garden` module's code? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: In the same file if the module is defined with a block instead of a semicolon
In src/garden.rs
In src/garden/mod.rs
Only in Cargo.toml

questions.explanation: The cheat sheet lists three forms: an inline block, src/garden.rs, and src/garden/mod.rs.

questions.text: What can `mod vegetables;` in `src/garden.rs` be used for?

answers.text: Declaring the `vegetables` submodule of the `garden` module
Importing an external crate named vegetables
Re-exporting every item in garden
Creating a new Cargo package

questions.explanation: A parent module file can declare submodules; `mod vegetables` tells the compiler about the child module.

source.section: Defining Modules to Control Scope and Privacy
source.locator: Chapter 7 — Defining Modules to Control Scope and Privacy, pp. 160–164

questions.text: Where can the code for submodule `vegetables`, declared in `src/garden.rs`, be located? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: In an inline block after mod vegetables
In src/garden/vegetables.rs
In src/garden/vegetables/mod.rs
Only in src/vegetables.rs

questions.explanation: For a child module, the compiler looks for an inline definition or a file under the parent module's directory.

questions.text: Which items can be inside a Rust module? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Functions
Structures and enums
Constants and traits
Only other modules, with no other item types

questions.explanation: A module can contain other modules as well as functions, structs, enums, constants, traits, and other definitions.

source.section: Defining Modules to Control Scope and Privacy
source.locator: Chapter 7 — Defining Modules to Control Scope and Privacy, pp. 160–164

questions.text: Which relationships exist between items in a module tree? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Modules defined within the same parent are siblings
A nested module is a child of its containing module
The containing module is the parent of the nested module
Every sibling is automatically public

questions.explanation: The chapter uses parent/child/sibling relationships to describe the tree; these relationships do not automatically change privacy.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Defining Modules to Control Scope and Privacy, pp. 160–164

questions.text: What does an absolute path to an item in the current crate begin with?

answers.text: `crate`
`super`
`self` necessarily
The name of the current function

questions.explanation: For an item in the current crate, an absolute path starts with `crate`. For an external crate, it starts with the external crate's name.

source.section: Paths for Referring to an Item in the Module Tree
source.locator: Chapter 7 — Paths for Referring to an Item in the Module Tree, pp. 165–166

questions.text: Which statements about relative paths are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: They start from the current module
They can begin with self
They can begin with super or an identifier in the current module
They must begin with crate

questions.explanation: Relative paths start from the current module and can use self, super, or a local identifier; crate indicates an absolute path in the current crate.

source.section: Paths for Referring to an Item in the Module Tree
source.locator: Chapter 7 — Paths for Referring to an Item in the Module Tree, pp. 165–166

questions.text: Why can code with a structurally correct path still fail to compile?

answers.text: Because one of the modules or items on the path may be private
Because Rust forbids paths longer than two segments
Because `crate` can only be used in main.rs
Because functions cannot be called through modules

questions.explanation: Path correctness and accessibility are separate checks. Listing 7-4 has a structurally correct path, but access is blocked by the private hosting module.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Exposing Paths with the `pub` Keyword, pp. 167–170

questions.text: Which privacy rules are stated for parent and child modules? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Items are private to parent modules by default
A parent cannot access private items in a child
A child can access items in its ancestor modules
Privacy prevents a child module from seeing its parent's context

questions.explanation: Privacy hides child-module details from outer ancestors, while child modules can see the context of their ancestors.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Exposing Paths with the `pub` Keyword, pp. 167–170

questions.text: What does `pub mod hosting` do?

answers.text: Makes the hosting module itself accessible but does not automatically make its contents public
Makes every function, structure, and field inside hosting public
Only imports hosting into the current scope
Creates a library crate named hosting

questions.explanation: `pub` on a module exposes the container. A function inside also needs its own `pub` to be publicly accessible.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Exposing Paths with the `pub` Keyword, pp. 167–170

questions.text: What is required for `crate::front_of_house::hosting::add_to_waitlist()` to pass privacy checks from an accessible context? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Access to front_of_house from the current module
hosting must be accessible along that path
add_to_waitlist must be public
The crate root itself must explicitly be declared public

questions.explanation: Every segment through which external code descends into child scopes must be accessible, and the function must be public. The crate root needs no separate annotation.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Exposing Paths with the `pub` Keyword, pp. 167–170

questions.text: Which benefits come from splitting a package into a library crate and a binary crate? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Other projects can reuse the library functionality
The binary crate uses the library's public API like an external user
The author simultaneously tests the usability of the public API from a user's perspective
The binary crate gains access to all private library items

questions.explanation: The binary crate acts as a separate consumer of the library API and sees only its public part, which helps design a good interface.

questions.text: What does `super::deliver_order()` mean inside a child module?

answers.text: Go to the parent module and find deliver_order there
Go to an external crate named super
Call a supertrait method
Make deliver_order public

questions.explanation: `super` starts a relative path from the parent module, similarly to `..` in a filesystem path.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Starting Relative Paths with `super`, pp. 171–172

questions.text: What happens to structure fields when declaring `pub struct Breakfast`?

answers.text: The structure itself becomes public, but fields remain private unless they also have `pub`
All fields automatically become public
The structure stays private until every field is public
Private fields are removed from the structure

questions.explanation: For a structure, `pub` exposes the type, but fields still follow the normal privacy rule and require their own `pub`.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Making Structs and Enums Public, pp. 172–174

questions.text: What happens to enum variants when the enum itself is declared `pub`?

answers.text: Its variants become public
Each variant still needs its own `pub`
The enum becomes private to its parent
Variants can only be used inside an impl

questions.explanation: Unlike structure fields, variants of a public enum are accessible without separate `pub` annotations.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Making Structs and Enums Public, pp. 172–174

questions.text: Which statements about `use` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `use` creates a convenient short name for a path in the current scope
The path introduced by `use` is still checked for accessibility
A `use` alias exists only in the scope where it is declared
`use` makes a private item public

questions.explanation: `use` shortens path notation but does not bypass privacy rules and has an ordinary scope.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Bringing Paths into Scope with `use`, pp. 175–180

questions.text: Why might `hosting::add_to_waitlist()` inside child module `customer` fail to see `hosting` if `use crate::front_of_house::hosting;` is written in the parent module?

answers.text: Because a name introduced by `use` is not automatically imported into a separate child scope
Because use works only in main
Because child modules can never see names in parents even through super
Because hosting must be an external crate

questions.explanation: A `use` declaration creates a name in its own scope. The child can import it again or refer to the parent's name through super.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Bringing Paths into Scope with `use`, pp. 175–180

questions.text: Which two fixes for the `use` scope problem are suggested for the `customer` module? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Move the use declaration inside customer
Refer to the parent's alias as super::hosting
Replace use with mod hosting without other changes
Make the main function public

questions.explanation: The material suggests importing the name in the required scope or referring to the name in the parent through super.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Bringing Paths into Scope with `use`, pp. 175–180

questions.text: Which statements about `use` idioms are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: For structures and enums, the full path to the type itself is usually imported
For functions, the parent module is usually imported
This is a readability convention rather than a compiler requirement
Rust forbids importing a structure directly

questions.explanation: The book distinguishes idioms for functions and types and emphasizes that this is a convention, not a syntax restriction.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Bringing Paths into Scope with `use`, pp. 175–180

questions.text: Which ways of working with two `Result` types from different modules are valid? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Import the parent modules and write `fmt::Result` and `io::Result`
Import one Result under an alias with as
Import both under the bare name Result into the same scope without renaming
Stop using both types entirely

questions.explanation: The material shows two idiomatic solutions: qualification through parent modules or aliasing one type.

questions.text: What does `pub use` do?

answers.text: Introduces a name into scope and re-exports it for external code
Only makes the current module private
Compiles the named file as a separate crate
Removes the item's original path

questions.explanation: `pub use` performs a re-export: the item is introduced locally and exposed to users through a new public path.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Bringing Paths into Scope with `use`, pp. 175–180

questions.text: Why can `pub use` re-exports be useful? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: They let the external API have a more convenient structure than the internal module organization
They can hide part of the internal path hierarchy from users
They let the library remain convenient for both authors and users
They automatically make all private fields of the re-exported type public

questions.explanation: A re-export separates internal module organization from the public path without changing privacy of the type's internal details.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Bringing Paths into Scope with `use`, pp. 175–180

questions.text: What is required to use an external package such as `rand`?

answers.text: Add the dependency to Cargo.toml and bring the required items into scope with use
Only write use without Cargo.toml
Copy rand's source code into src
Rename the package to std

questions.explanation: Cargo must know about the external dependency, after which its items can be brought into scope with use.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Bringing Paths into Scope with `use`, pp. 175–180

questions.text: Which statements about the standard library `std` in the context of `use` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `std` is a crate external to our package
`std` does not need to be added to Cargo.toml because it ships with Rust
Some `std` items are still brought into scope with use
`std` can only be used from a library crate

questions.explanation: The standard library ships with Rust, so Cargo.toml need not change, but its items may still be brought into scope through use.

source.locator: Chapter 7 — Bringing Paths into Scope with `use`, pp. 175–180

questions.text: Which capabilities do nested `use` paths support? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Combining imports with a shared prefix
Using `self` when one import is the shared path itself
Reducing the number of separate use lines
Changing private/public access rules

questions.explanation: Nested use is a compact notation for imports and does not affect privacy.

answers.text: Bring both `std::io` and `std::io::Write` into scope
Bring only Write into scope and ignore self
Make io public
Declare a Write submodule inside io

It can make the origin of names harder to understand
The book notes that it is often used in tests and prelude-like patterns
It makes private items public

answers.text: Declare the module and let the compiler find its code in the corresponding file

The module code moves to src/front_of_house.rs

In target/hosting.rs
At the project root next to Cargo.toml, outside src
